learningObjectives.title: Processes and causes of rural change

questions.q: What does the term 'rural-urban continuum' describe?
options: A sudden dividing line between town and countryside
The gradual change in settlement character from remote rural to inner-city urban
A government policy limiting rural building
The migration of farmers into cities
questions.explain: The rural-urban continuum recognises there is no sharp boundary but a gradation of settlement types from remote rural to fully urban.

questions.q: A settlement close to a city where many residents travel into the city to work is best described as a:
options: Commuter (dormitory) village
Honeypot site
Remote hamlet
Shanty settlement
questions.explain: Commuter or dormitory villages house people who work in a nearby city and return to sleep, giving the settlement a suburbanised character.

questions.q: Counter-urbanisation is the movement of people:
options: From rural areas into large cities
From cities and larger towns into rural areas
Between different countries for work
From one city centre to another
questions.explain: Counter-urbanisation is the migration of people away from urban areas towards rural and accessible rural settlements.

questions.q: Which term describes large-scale, capital-intensive commercial farming run like a business, often by companies?
options: Subsistence farming
Agribusiness
Crofting
Shifting cultivation
questions.explain: Agribusiness is large-scale commercial farming organised for maximum efficiency and profit, typically using heavy machinery and capital investment.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of farm diversification?
options: Increasing the size of fields by removing hedgerows
Opening a farm shop and holiday accommodation
Buying larger tractors to plough faster
Switching from wheat to barley
questions.explain: Diversification means generating income from non-traditional activities such as farm shops, camping or holiday lets alongside farming.

questions.q: Rural deprivation most commonly refers to:
options: A lack of access to services, jobs and affordable housing in rural areas
Overcrowding in rural tower blocks
Excessive industrial pollution in the countryside
A shortage of farmland for crops
questions.explain: Rural deprivation is the poor access to services, employment, transport and housing that disadvantages some rural residents.

questions.q: A 'honeypot site' in a rural area is a place that:
options: Produces most of the region's honey
Attracts large numbers of tourists and visitors
Has been abandoned by all residents
Is protected from any public access
questions.explain: A honeypot site is a scenic or historic location that draws many tourists, concentrating visitor pressure in one area.

questions.q: Which pair best describes typical land use in a rural area?
options: High-rise offices and factories
Agriculture, forestry and open countryside
Container ports and rail terminals
Dense terraced housing and shopping malls
questions.explain: Rural areas are dominated by primary land uses such as farming and forestry together with open, undeveloped countryside.

questions.q: Why does counter-urbanisation often change the social character of a village?
options: It reduces the total population to zero
Incoming wealthier commuters raise house prices and may not use local services
It forces all farmers to leave the area
It causes the village to be reclassified as a city
questions.explain: Newcomers can push up house prices beyond locals' reach and, working elsewhere, may support services less than long-standing residents.

questions.q: Why do many young adults migrate away from remote rural areas?
options: There are too many schools and universities
Limited job opportunities and higher education force them to move
Rural areas have no housing at all
They are legally required to leave at 18
questions.explain: A shortage of well-paid jobs and further/higher education pushes young people towards urban areas, leaving an ageing population behind.

questions.q: An ageing population in a remote rural area is often the combined result of:
options: High birth rates and immigration of families
Out-migration of the young and in-migration of retirees
A ban on people over 60 moving in
Rapid industrial growth attracting workers
questions.explain: Young people leave for work while retirees move in for a quieter lifestyle, raising the average age of the population.

questions.q: How can a high proportion of second homes affect a rural community?
options: It guarantees local shops stay open all year
It can raise house prices and leave the village quiet outside holiday periods
It always increases the permanent local population
It reduces the average age of residents
questions.explain: Second homes inflate prices for locals and, being empty much of the year, reduce year-round demand that keeps services viable.

questions.q: How has increased mechanisation of agriculture affected rural areas?
options: It has greatly increased the number of farm labourers
It has reduced farm employment, contributing to rural depopulation
It has stopped all crop production
It has forced farms to become much smaller
questions.explain: Machines replace manual labour, cutting farm jobs and encouraging workers to migrate away from the countryside.

questions.q: Why do accessible rural areas near cities tend to grow in population while remote rural areas decline?
options: Remote areas have better broadband and transport
Accessible areas allow people to commute to urban jobs while enjoying countryside living
Governments forbid people living in remote areas
Accessible areas have no farmland
questions.explain: Good transport links let residents work in the city yet live rurally, so accessible villages attract growth that remote ones cannot.

questions.q: Which is a common consequence of falling population in a remote village?
options: An increase in the number of bus routes
Closure of services such as shops, post offices and schools
A rise in traffic congestion
Rapid building of new offices
questions.explain: As population and demand fall, services become uneconomic and close, further reducing the village's attractiveness — a spiral of decline.

questions.q: Which strategy would best help make rural service provision more sustainable in a declining village?
options: Closing the last bus service completely
Providing mobile services such as a mobile library or a bus-based post office
Banning all newcomers from the village
Demolishing the village shop
questions.explain: Mobile and shared services deliver essential provision at lower cost where a permanent facility is no longer viable.

questions.q: A national park suffers footpath erosion and traffic jams at a popular viewpoint. Which management response is most appropriate?
options: Encourage even more cars by removing all car parks
Build a motorway through the park centre
Introduce park-and-ride buses and lay durable, marked footpaths
Ban all residents from the area
questions.explain: Park-and-ride cuts traffic pressure while surfaced, marked paths concentrate and reduce erosion at honeypot sites.

questions.q: A hill farmer's income from sheep has fallen sharply. Which option is an example of sustainable diversification rather than intensification?
options: Removing hedgerows to create one huge field
Converting a barn into holiday cottages and offering guided walks
Doubling the flock size and using more fertiliser
Ploughing up moorland to grow more crops
questions.explain: Diversifying into tourism generates new income while conserving the landscape, unlike intensification that can damage the environment.

questions.q: A village near a large city has gained new estates, its farm cottages are now owned by commuters, and the bus service is busy at rush hour. This village is best classified as:
options: A remote depopulating hamlet
A suburbanised (commuter) village
An unspoilt subsistence-farming settlement
An abandoned ghost village
questions.explain: New housing, commuter ownership and rush-hour transport demand are the classic signs of a suburbanised village experiencing counter-urbanisation.

questions.q: Local people cannot afford homes in a scenic village dominated by second homes. Which measure most directly tackles this challenge?
options: Allowing unlimited second-home purchases
Building affordable homes reserved for local residents
Closing the village school to save money
Encouraging more tourists to buy property
questions.explain: Affordable housing schemes tied to local occupancy help retain residents and keep community services viable.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Geography (4GE1) specification; Rural Environments
